\chapter{Calling Somebody, and Asking Again}
\label{ch:ar-calling-somebody-and-asking-again}
\hlchaptermodality{41}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can call somebody by name with \ar{يا}, ask them to say it again with \ar{كرّر} \ar{من} \ar{فضلك}, and run the whole first meeting of chapters one to four with the repair kit inside it.}

The greeting, name and wellbeing exchanges of chapters 1-4 -- untouched for more than a hundred lessons -- are run cold and then broken on purpose, so the learner uses \ar{عفوا}, \ar{لا} \ar{أفهم} and \ar{كرّر} \ar{من} \ar{فضلك} to get the conversation back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yā]{\ar{يا} (yā) — calling somebody}

\label{lesson:AR-C41-ya}



\begin{quote}
Chapter two taught you to give your name and to ask for somebody else's. Forty chapters later you still cannot \textbf{call} them by it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the time joiner from the lesson before — \emph{ḥīnamā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{يا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{حسن}} — \emph{yā Ḥasan} — \textbf{Hasan!} (calling him)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{جار}} — \emph{yā jār} — \textbf{neighbour!}
\end{quote}

Arabic does not address a person with a bare name. \textbf{\ar{حسن}} on its own is a statement \emph{about} Hasan; \textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{حسن}} is speaking \emph{to} him. The particle is not optional politeness — it is how the language marks the difference between naming somebody and calling them.

Two letters, both long since yours, and no ending changes on the name.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{يا}} is pan-Semitic and English has no particle of its own to match it. The one place English reaches for something similar is old translation — \emph{O Lord}, \emph{O Israel} — where the \emph{O} is standing in for exactly this. It sounds archaic in English and is entirely everyday in Arabic.

It goes before a title or a kin term as readily as before a name: \textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{ابن}}, \textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{بنت}}, \emph{yā ṣadīqī}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{yā Ḥasan}
  \item \emph{yā jār} … \emph{yā ṣadīqī}
  \item the name alone, then called — \emph{Ḥasan} … \emph{yā Ḥasan}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between \textbf{\ar{حسن}} and \textbf{\ar{يا} \ar{حسن}}? (\textbf{One names him; the other calls him}.) Does the name change shape after it? (\textbf{No}.) And what does English use where Arabic uses \textbf{\ar{يا}}? (\textbf{Nothing, ordinarily} — only \emph{O} in old translation.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karrir min faḍlik]{\ar{كرّر} \ar{من} \ar{فضلك} — say it again, please}

\label{lesson:AR-C41-karrir}



\begin{quote}
Chapter thirty-seven gave you the first thing a lost learner says. Saying it only helps if you can also ask for the sentence back.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the particle from the lesson before, and what it turns a name into — \emph{yā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{كرّر}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كرّر}} — \emph{karrir} — \textbf{repeat.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كرّر} \ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} — \emph{karrir min faḍlik} — \textbf{say it again, please.}
\end{quote}

The \emph{please} is not new: chapter six taught it. What is new is the verb, and the shape it comes in — this is the first \textbf{command} in the book, and Arabic builds one by stripping the present tense back to its bare stem.

Look at the shadda. \textbf{\ar{كرّر}} doubles its middle letter, which is the same Form II shape as \emph{fakkara} in chapter thirty-two — a pattern that means \emph{do it thoroughly, do it repeatedly}. On the root \ar{ك}-\ar{ر}-\ar{ر}, \textquotedblleft{}to return\textquotedblright{}, that gives exactly \emph{do it again}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the repair kit, whole}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{say} \\
\midrule
you did not follow & \emph{lā afham} \\
you want it again & \emph{karrir min faḍlik} \\
you are grateful for it & \emph{shukran} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The inventory that measured this track said the repair kit was strong with one hole in it: sorry, excuse me, pardon, please and thank you were all taught, and \emph{I do not understand} and \emph{say it again} were not. Those two are what chapters thirty-seven and forty-one add, and between them they needed one new verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{karrir}
  \item \emph{karrir min faḍlik}
  \item the whole kit in order — \emph{lā afham … karrir min faḍlik … shukran}
  \item and get their attention first — \emph{yā Ḥasan, karrir min faḍlik}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which chapter taught the \emph{please} in this sentence? (\textbf{Six}.) Which earlier verb wears the same doubled shape? (\emph{\textbf{fakkara}}, chapter thirty-two.) And what does that shape add to a root? (\textbf{Doing it thoroughly, or again}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yā · karrir min faḍlik]{Calling somebody, and asking again}

\label{lesson:AR-R41-calling-and-asking-again}



\begin{quote}
Two items landed in this chapter: one gets somebody's attention and one asks them for the sentence back. Name both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yā Ḥasan, karrir min faḍlik}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the reason you are asking — \emph{lā afham li-annanī lā asmaʿ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} four lessons back, the particle that fronts a question — \emph{hal}
  \item \emph{Recall:} nine lessons back, the word that accepts what was said — \emph{ḥasanan}
  \item \emph{Recall:} five lessons back, ask why, then report the answer — \emph{limādhā?} … \emph{aktub anna …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} ten lessons back, refuse both at once — \emph{lā shāy wa-lā ḥalīb}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the first meeting, and what to do when it goes wrong}
The exchange this book opened with was taught more than a hundred lessons ago and has not been asked for since. It is also the exact place a beginner loses the thread. Run it cold, and put the new chapter inside it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the greeting and its reply, and hear the \textbf{\ar{و}} at the front of the reply — \emph{as-salāmu ʿalaykum} … \emph{wa-ʿalaykum as-salām}
  \item the name exchange — \emph{mā ismuka?} … \emph{ismī …} … \emph{tasharrafnā}
  \item the wellbeing exchange — \emph{kayfa ḥāluka?} … \emph{bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu li-llāh}
  \item now lose the thread and rescue it — \emph{ʿafwan, lā afham. karrir min faḍlik}
  \item thank them, and close — \emph{shukran} … \emph{maʿa s-salāma}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Five chapters ago this book could not say a verb in the present, deny a nominal sentence, join two nouns, ask a yes-or-no question, give a reason, or say that it had not understood. Say the sentence that was one tense away for thirty-one chapters. (\emph{\textbf{lā afham}}.) Say what you ask next. (\emph{\textbf{karrir min faḍlik}}.) And say how you get somebody's attention first. (\emph{\textbf{yā}} \textbf{plus their name}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
